title: Reading the Rings of Trees
topic: How tree rings became a dating method precise to a single year
passage:
Cut across the trunk of a tree in a temperate forest and the history of its life is laid out in concentric circles. Each ring is one growing season: a band of large, thin-walled cells formed in spring when water is plentiful, followed by a band of smaller, denser cells laid down as the season closes. The boundary between the dense wood of one year and the open wood of the next is sharp enough to count, and counting is where the science of dendrochronology begins. It does not, however, end there, and the interesting work has never been about age.

The width of a ring records how good the year was. A season with ample rain and mild temperatures produces a wide band; a drought produces a narrow one. Because every tree in a region experiences the same weather, trees growing near one another produce the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, in the same order. That shared pattern is a signature, and it can be matched between samples in the way that a torn page can be matched to the book it came from.

This is what allows the record to reach back far beyond the life of any single tree. A living oak felled today might carry three hundred rings. A beam in a medieval roof, taken from a tree cut down long ago, will carry its own sequence, and if the outermost rings of the beam overlap with the innermost rings of the living tree, the two sequences can be joined. Repeat the process with older and older timber and the chain extends backwards, century by century. Chronologies built this way now run continuously for more than ten thousand years in parts of Europe, assembled from living trees, building timbers and wood preserved in bogs and riverbeds.

The method has an unusual property for a dating technique: it produces a calendar year, not a range. Radiocarbon dating returns a probability spread of a century or more; a matched ring sequence returns a specific year, and sometimes a season within it, because the last ring formed before felling shows whether the tree was cut in summer or in winter. That precision has been used to date the construction of buildings, the timbers of ships, and the panels behind paintings whose attribution was disputed. A panel cannot have been painted before the tree it came from was felled, which has quietly ended a number of arguments.

The technique also records events that were not weather. A frost ring, its cells crushed and discoloured, marks a cold snap severe enough to freeze living tissue during the growing season. A run of exceptionally narrow rings across a whole continent points to something that dimmed the sun, and several such runs align with the dates of large volcanic eruptions known from ice cores. The most famous of these, in the years following 536, appears in trees from Europe to Asia and coincides with written accounts of a dimmed sun and failed harvests. Dendrochronology did not discover that event, but it established its scale.

There are limits, and they are worth stating. The method works only where growth is genuinely seasonal, which excludes most tropical species, whose growth is governed by rainfall patterns that may produce two rings in a year or none. It requires wood that has not rotted, so the record is biased towards dry climates, waterlogged deposits and buildings that survived. And a single sample is nearly useless: a tree shaded by a neighbour, or damaged, or growing on a slope, produces a pattern that reflects its own circumstances rather than the region's, so a reliable chronology needs many trees and a statistical judgement about which ones agree.

What has changed most recently is the resolution. Techniques that measure the density of the late wood, or the ratio of oxygen isotopes within a single ring, extract a climate signal from trees whose ring widths are too uniform to be informative — including some tropical species previously thought unusable. The old work counted rings and measured them. The new work reads the chemistry inside them, and in doing so has begun to recover a seasonal record of climate from regions that had none.

questions.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage? Write TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, or NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

questions.statement: The cells formed at the end of a growing season are smaller than those formed in spring.
questions.explanation: The passage describes “large, thin-walled cells formed in spring” followed by “smaller, denser cells laid down as the season closes”.

questions.statement: Trees growing close together produce different ring patterns from one another.
questions.explanation: The opposite is stated: “trees growing near one another produce the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, in the same order”, because they share the same weather.

questions.statement: Radiocarbon dating is cheaper than dendrochronology.
questions.explanation: The passage compares the two only on precision — a probability spread against a calendar year. Cost is never mentioned for either method.

questions.statement: Most tropical trees produce one clear ring each year.
questions.explanation: The passage says tropical growth “may produce two rings in a year or none”, which is why most tropical species are excluded from the standard method.

questions.statement: A chronology can be built reliably from a single well-preserved tree.
questions.explanation: “A single sample is nearly useless”, because shading, damage or slope make one tree reflect its own circumstances; a reliable chronology “needs many trees”.

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.sentence: Sequences from living trees and old timbers can be joined where their rings ___.
questions.explanation: “If the outermost rings of the beam overlap with the innermost rings of the living tree, the two sequences can be joined.”

questions.sentence: European chronologies now run continuously for more than ___ years.
questions.explanation: “Chronologies built this way now run continuously for more than ten thousand years in parts of Europe.” The figure is given in words in the passage.

questions.sentence: Crushed, discoloured cells forming a ___ show that tissue froze during the growing season.
questions.explanation: “A frost ring, its cells crushed and discoloured, marks a cold snap severe enough to freeze living tissue during the growing season.”

questions.sentence: Narrow rings across a continent have been matched with eruption dates recorded in ___.
questions.explanation: “Several such runs align with the dates of large volcanic eruptions known from ice cores.” The ice cores are the independent source.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.question: Why does the writer compare ring patterns to a torn page?
options: To show that samples are easily damaged
To explain how one sequence is matched to another
To suggest that early records were written on wood
To argue that the method is unreliable
questions.explanation: The shared pattern “can be matched between samples in the way that a torn page can be matched to the book it came from” — the image is about matching, not fragility.

questions.question: What can the outermost ring of a felled tree reveal?
options: The age of the forest around it
The season in which it was cut
questions.explanation: “The last ring formed before felling shows whether the tree was cut in summer or in winter”, which is how the method reaches a season as well as a year.

questions.question: What does the writer say about the event of 536?
options: Dendrochronology was the first evidence of it
Tree rings established how widespread it was
It has since been shown not to have happened
questions.explanation: “Dendrochronology did not discover that event, but it established its scale”, with the signal appearing in trees “from Europe to Asia”.

questions.question: What is new about recent work in the field?
options: It counts rings more accurately than before
It reads chemical signals within a ring
It has abandoned the use of building timbers
It no longer requires many samples
questions.explanation: “The old work counted rings and measured them. The new work reads the chemistry inside them”, using late-wood density and oxygen isotope ratios.
